name: Twin Sisters Olivine Scramble
prior_findings: The row mixes a Class 3-4 scramble with the 5.4 north ridge; both lines exist. Split, or pick one and rewrite the other fields.

earlier_research.fact: Approach: Skookum Pasture logging road vs Elbow Lake Trail / Green Creek
earlier_research.correct_value: Approach is the Elbow Lake Trail (north trailhead, FR 38), ford of the Middle Fork Nooksack, then the blazed Green Creek climbers' path into the Green Creek Cirque; no logging-road/timberland-gate approach.
earlier_research.evidence: A Green Creek Circuit trip report starts at the Elbow Lake Trailhead, crosses the Middle Fork Nooksack and follows the blue-marked Green Creek climbers' trail into the cirque before reaching Skookum via Jaws' Tooth. A separate guide-service trip report gives the same approach: FR 38 to the Elbow Lake trailhead (2,100 ft), river crossing, then leaving the trail at a switchback near Hildebrand Creek into Green Creek. The 'Skookum Pasture logging road' could not be found anywhere; the bike-the-logging-road text matches the west-side Dailey Prairie approach to the Twin Sisters and was copied from another route. Ridge-specific beta in the same itinerary note ('stay left/west of the crest', 2nd-3rd class) is also likely copied but is tied to the unresolved grade question and was left untouched.

earlier_research.fact: Grade: Class 3-4 scramble vs 5.4 north ridge
earlier_research.evidence: Sources agree Skookum's north ridge, reached by rappelling off Jaws' Tooth, is 5.4 on solid olivine (Green Creek Circuit trip report; the circuit overall is rated IV 5.6). No source documents a standalone Class 3-4 'standard' route up Skookum; the only non-technical terrain described is the loose south/southwest face used as a descent on the circuit. Whether this row is the 5.4 north ridge or a Class 3-4 scramble is a route-identity decision (name and discipline say scramble; beta, face, rock_grade and pro_needs describe the north ridge), so no patch.

One trip report confirms a ~15 m rappel off Jaws' Tooth to reach Skookum's north ridge, for which a 30 m rope barely suffices. Whether rope_type 'none' or pro_needs' 30 m rope is right depends on whether this row is the north ridge or a scramble, which is unresolved above.

earlier_research.fact: Descent: reverse vs committing past Jaws' Tooth
earlier_research.evidence: Both circuit sources descend Skookum by its south/southwest face (described as loose) toward the col east of Hayden, not by reversing the north ridge; reversing would mean re-climbing Jaws' Tooth. The row, however, explicitly warns against the south slopes. Which descent applies depends on the unresolved route identity, and changing a safety-relevant descent needs that settled first.

earlier_research.correct_value: The Green Creek climbers' path leaves the Elbow Lake Trail at a switchback near Hildebrand Creek, about 1.5 miles past the river crossing — not at Elbow Lake after ~8 miles.
earlier_research.evidence: A guide-service trip report puts the departure from the Elbow Lake trail at a switchback (~2,650 ft) about 1.5 miles after the Middle Fork crossing, near Hildebrand Creek. A range overview and the circuit trip report likewise describe a blazed climbers' trail branching off the Elbow Lake trail at a switchback near Hildebrand Creek; the row's own junction waypoint agrees. Round-trip mileage was not settled: whole-circuit sources give 11-13 miles, below both the itinerary's 14 and watch_out's ~16, so those figures and dist_km were left alone.

No source states a car-to-car gain for Skookum alone; the only published totals are for the full Green Creek Circuit (7,000-8,000 ft). Per the rules gain_ft is not recomputed from pin arithmetic. The summit elevation itself is also disputed across sources (see discovered entry).

earlier_research.correct_value: The unofficial log/rope crossing was destroyed in the December 2025 floods and not replaced.
earlier_research.evidence: A June 2026 regional news report states the log crossing with rope handrails at the Elbow Lake Trailhead was lost in the December storms, with no repair timeline for FSR 38. hazards, pro_tips, approach and access.closures on the row all agree; only the waypoint note still told climbers to use the rig.

Sources disagree: a range overview gives 6,616 ft, the state geographic-names proposal summary for Kloke Peak gives 6,480 ft, and a climbing database lists 5,962 ft; none matches the row's 6,534. No two independent topo-derived figures agree, so no change.

Two independent sources now agree on the north-ridge facts: a route page says you rappel south off Jaw's Tooth to the Skookum notch from a tat anchor (or downclimb low 5th) and then climb low-5th ridge to Skookum's top, descending 3rd-class gullies on the south side; a separate trip report describes tying back in for the exposed north ridge. So beta/pro_needs (rope, rappel) are right for the north ridge, and rope_type 'none' would be right only for a separate scramble line. The row mixes both (name/grade 'Olivine Scramble' Class 3-4 vs face 'North Ridge', rock_grade 5.4), so which rope fields are wrong depends on which route the row is; no minimal patch settles it. Would settle: an owner decision on whether this row is the north ridge (then rope_type/rope_note/gear change) or the south-side scramble (then beta/pro_needs/face/rock_grade change).

The row is internally consistent (high_point_ft and the summit pin both 6,534). The USGS 1 m point-elevation service reads 6,533.9 ft exactly at the summit pin, and a grid of samples 40-120 m around it all read 6,140-6,360 ft, so the pin sits on the lidar high point. The published 6,480 (state names proposal) and 6,500 (topo list) are 40-ft contour-map figures, and 6,616/5,962 elsewhere refer to other points; nothing supports changing the stored value.

descent_text, hazards and watch_out say never descend Skookum's south-facing slopes, while a route page for the Jaw's Tooth/north ridge line gives the descent as 3rd-class gullies down the south side of the mountain. Only one source states the descent, and it is tied to the route-identity question above. Would settle: a second report of the Skookum descent plus the owner's decision on which route this row describes.

earlier_research.correct_value: ~14 miles round trip
earlier_research.evidence: Four row fields agree on 14 mi (itinerary miles, totalNote, dist_km 22.53 km, summit pin 7 mi one-way); only watch_out says ~16. Externally the whole five-summit Green Creek Circuit from the same trailhead is about 13 mi (Mountain Project) / 11-13 mi (a 2021 trip report), so a Skookum-only round trip of ~16 mi is too high; ~14 is the closer figure.

earlier_research.fact: Which side of the crest to stay on
earlier_research.evidence: Real: travelling south, climber's left is east, so 'left/west' cannot both be right. The only published descriptions of Skookum from this side are of the 5.4 north ridge, which stays on the crest; none describe a Class 3-4 side-of-crest line, and the row's own pins put the summit west-northwest of the ridge gain point, not south. Settling it needs a description of the scramble line naming which flank it uses.

earlier_research.correct_value: Jul-Sep
earlier_research.evidence: best_season, itinerary.cal and climate.summer all say July-September and the guidance marks July optimal; only the header says 'Late Jul'. Green Creek Circuit parties have climbed these summits as early as late June (trip reports dated 22 Jun 2013 and 30 Jun 2019), so July is in season. Also removed a doubled 'September-September' typo in optimalWindow.

earlier_research.fact: Time from the trail junction to the ridge crest
earlier_research.evidence: Real: +1 hr for ~4 mi and ~3,400 ft through the cirque and loose 3rd/4th class is implausible, while +2-3 hr for the first 2.5 mi of maintained trail is slow. One 2021 party reached the base of the Green Creek Arete in the cirque about 2 hr after leaving the car, but no source gives junction-to-crest or car-to-crest times for this line. Settling needs a timed trip report to the Skookum ridge from the Green Creek path.

row.name: Twin Sisters Olivine Scramble
row.fa: Dallas Kloke and Dave Dixon, September 1972 (first ascent of the peak)
hazards: Unbridged/washed-out Middle Fork Nooksack River crossing near the Elbow Lake trailhead (log/rope crossing destroyed in Dec 2025 floods)
Loose, choss-filled rock on Skookum's south-facing slopes — avoid for descent
Exposed, knife-edge ridge scrambling with substantial fall potential, especially on the north ridge variation
row.overview: Skookum Peak is one of the summits of the Twin Sisters Range west of Mount Baker, a chain famous for its reddish-orange olivine (dunite) rock — a rare exposed fragment of the earth's mantle and the largest such body in the Western Hemisphere. The peak lies on the ridge system extending south from South Twin, the range highpoint, and is a highlight of the popular east-side Green Creek Circuit linkup with South Twin, Jaws' Tooth, Little Sister, and Cinderella. It is also known unofficially as 'Kloke Peak': in 2022 Washington's Committee on Geographic Names took up a proposal to formally rename it after Anacortes climber Dallas Kloke, who with Dave Dixon made the first recorded ascent in September 1972 and put up a dozen new routes across the Twin Sisters through the 1980s before his death in a 2010 North Cascades climbing accident. Both names are still used interchangeably by climbers (commonly written 'Skookum (Kloke)').
row.beta: The north ridge climbs sustained but famously 'bomber' red dunite/olivine rock rated 5.4, with immense exposure on knife-edge sections; climbers work along small ledges, shuffling hands on positive edges. It is reached by rappelling off the adjacent Jaws' Tooth rather than climbed as a stand-alone route, and continues onward toward Little Sister as one leg of the range's classic 'Green Creek Circuit' traverse.
row.turnaround: Because the line is committing once past Jaws' Tooth, turn back (or reconsider starting) before that point if conditions, party pace, or weather put finishing the full ridge traverse and the river crossing back at the trailhead in question — there is no fast retreat from Skookum itself.
row.permit: No climbing permit; a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Elbow Lake Trail's north trailhead.
obj_haz: long approach with an unbridged river ford

waypoints.name: Elbow Lake Trail - North Trailhead (FR 38)
waypoints.note: Low-elevation trailhead off FR 38 via Mosquito Lake Rd; Northwest Forest Pass required, and FR 38 is gated Dec 1-Jun 15 at Wallace Creek. This is a separate trailhead from 'Pioneer Camp,' which sits at the trail's south end off Baker Lake Highway/FSR 12.
waypoints.directions: From the Mount Baker Ranger District office in Sedro-Woolley, drive north on WA-9 to Acme and turn right (east) onto Mosquito Lake Road for about 9 miles, crossing the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then continue onto Forest Road 38 for roughly 11 miles to the north trailhead for the Elbow Lake Trail at about 2,000 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and FR 38 is gated at Wallace Creek from December 1 through June 15. Do not confuse this with the Pioneer Camp trailhead, which sits at the trail's south end off the Baker Lake Highway (FSR 12). As of mid-2026 FR 38 was damaged in the December 2025 floods with no published repair date, so confirm current road conditions with the Mount Baker Ranger District before you drive in.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Nooksack River crossing
waypoints.note: No bridge on this side — the unofficial log crossing with rope handrails was destroyed in the December 2025 floods and has not been replaced, so this is a ford that can be unfordable at high flow.

waypoints.name: Green Creek climbers' path junction (Hildebrand Creek switchback)
waypoints.note: Unmaintained, sparsely blue-blazed climbers' trail for Green Creek Cirque splits off the maintained Elbow Lake Trail #697 at a switchback near Hildebrand Creek — easy to walk past, watch for paint blazes and flagging.

waypoints.name: Green Creek at the cirque mouth
waypoints.note: Green Creek runs clear here at the entrance to the Green Creek Cirque — treat this as the last reliable water before the upper slabs and summit ridge.

waypoints.name: Connecting ridge gain point south of South Twin
waypoints.note: Loose, engaging 3rd/4th-class scrambling out of the cirque gains the ridge crest just south of South Twin; from here the route turns south along the connecting ridge to Skookum on grippy olivine.

waypoints.name: Skookum Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit (also known as 'Kloke Peak'); descend by reversing the ridge and climbers' path back to the Green Creek Cirque.

sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Car-to-car: Elbow Lake Trail and Green Creek Cirque + olivine ridge scramble

what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass for the trailhead
30m rope plus a small rack (finger-to-hand cams, slings) if attempting the 5.4 north ridge or linking into the full Green Creek Circuit
Approach shoes are adequate for the standard Class 3-4 line
Ice axe useful into early summer on lingering north-aspect snow
pro_tips: Standard access to Skookum is from the east via Elbow Lake Trail #697 and the Green Creek climbers' path — not the Dailey Prairie/west-side roads used for North and South Twin
Confirm the Elbow Lake trailhead river crossing is actually passable before committing — the log/rope crossing washed out in the December 2025 floods and has not been rebuilt
The olivine is famously grippy (like coarse sandpaper) on the ridges but loose and rotten on south-facing slopes — pick your ascent/descent line accordingly
A harder, more direct alternative is Skookum's north ridge (5.4) — reportedly an exposed, knife-edged line on bomber rock with immense exposure.
watch_out: South faces are loose scree and rockfall-prone — descend the way you came up, not down the south side
Long approach (~14 miles round trip via Elbow Lake Trail) with real elevation gain before any climbing begins
FSR 38 has been closed since the December 2025 floods with no published repair date — check current Mount Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts before you drive out
row.pro_needs: A light rack for protecting 5.4 moves on generally solid, positive rock; a 30m rope is carried for the rappel off Jaws' Tooth immediately before this section.
row.best_season: July through September is the reliable window: rock is dry and at its grippiest, though north-aspect gullies and the approach can hold lingering snow into early July in heavy-snowpack years, and late-summer afternoons can bring thunderstorms or wildfire smoke. Road access overrides season as the limiting factor — FSR 38 has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since July 27, 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on September 26, 2026, so check Mount Baker Ranger District alerts regardless of time of year.
row.approach: From the Mount Baker Ranger District office in Sedro-Woolley, drive north on WA-9 to Acme, turn right (east) on Mosquito Lake Road for about 9 miles, cross the Middle Fork Nooksack River, and continue onto Forest Road 38 for roughly 11 miles to the Elbow Lake Trail's north trailhead (a separate trailhead from 'Pioneer Camp,' which is actually on the trail's south end via Baker Lake Highway/FSR 12). From there, follow Elbow Lake Trail #697 across the Middle Fork Nooksack and up to a switchback near Hildebrand Creek, then pick up the unmaintained Green Creek climbers' path into the Green Creek Cirque beneath Skookum's north/east flank before gaining the ridge. This whole approach is compromised: FSR 38 was damaged in the December 2025 floods and has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since 27 July 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on 25 September 2026, and the unofficial log crossing with rope handrails over the Middle Fork Nooksack near the trailhead was also washed out — confirm current conditions with the Mount Baker Ranger District before driving in.
row.descent_text: Descend by retracing the ascent ridge rather than dropping into the south-facing gullies and slopes, which are loose, choss-filled rock and a significant rockfall hazard to parties below. From the Green Creek Cirque, return via the climbers' path to the Elbow Lake Trail and out to the trailhead.
row.bail: Descend the ridge into the Green Creek Cirque and walk out via the climbers' path and the Elbow Lake Trail.

itinerary.cal: Best done once the brushy approach and ridge are fully snow-free, typically mid-summer through early fall (roughly July-September).

days.note: This is a big single-day outing, not a backpack: parties hike the Elbow Lake Trail, ford the Middle Fork Nooksack and follow the blazed Green Creek climbers' path into the Green Creek Cirque, then scramble loose third and fourth class ground out of the cirque onto the ridge where the terrain turns to famously grippy olivine/dunite rock. The ridge itself is mostly 2nd-3rd class if you stay left/west of the crest, with short 3rd-4th class steps and real exposure near the top; route-finding (staying left, not straying right onto harder terrain) is the crux of the day as much as the climbing.
days.title: Car-to-car: Elbow Lake Trail and Green Creek Cirque + olivine ridge scramble

schedule.label: Leave the trailhead
schedule.detail: Start hiking in the dark to bank time; the Middle Fork Nooksack ford comes within the first quarter mile.

schedule.label: Leave the trail for the Green Creek path
schedule.detail: At a switchback near Hildebrand Creek the blazed climbers' path leaves the maintained trail and heads into the Green Creek Cirque.

schedule.label: Gain the ridge crest
schedule.detail: Forest opens onto exposed olivine/dunite rock; keep left (west side) of the crest for easier going.

schedule.label: Scramble to the summit
schedule.detail: 3rd-4th class sections with exposure; most parties top out by late morning to early afternoon.

schedule.label: Begin descent
schedule.detail: Reverse the ridge and downclimb carefully - loose rock and exposure demand as much care going down as up.

schedule.label: Back at the car
schedule.detail: Retrace the Green Creek path and the Elbow Lake Trail, fording the Middle Fork again on the way out.

days.objective: Summit Skookum Peak via the Elbow Lake Trail, the Green Creek Cirque and the olivine (dunite) ridge

itinerary.totalNote: A long but standard single day: roughly 9-11 hours car-to-car, ~14 miles round trip and ~4,200 ft of gain, mixing a long trail and climbers'-path approach with 2nd-4th class ridge scrambling on grippy olivine rock.

approach_variants.name: Green Creek Cirque and the ridge from South Twin
approach_variants.notes: From the north trailhead of the Elbow Lake Trail, follow the maintained trail across the Middle Fork and up to a switchback near Hildebrand Creek, where the unmaintained, sparsely blue-blazed Green Creek climbers' path leaves it — it is easy to walk past. The path climbs into the Green Creek Cirque; treat the creek at the cirque mouth as the last reliable water. Loose third and fourth class scrambling out of the cirque gains the ridge crest just south of South Twin, and the route then follows the connecting ridge south. The road and the river crossing at the trailhead have both been damaged by flooding, so confirm access before driving in.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn, once the cirque slabs are dry
hazards: Unbridged Middle Fork crossing at the trailhead, unfordable at high flow
Loose third and fourth class ground gaining the ridge out of the cirque
Immense exposure on the knife-edge sections of the ridge itself
approach_variants.baseFinding: Skookum sits on the ridge running SOUTH from South Twin, and the tower immediately north of it is Jaws' Tooth — a slender detached spire that reads as a tooth rather than a summit and is the single best identifier on this stretch of crest. The base of Skookum's north ridge is the notch on the far, southern side of that tooth, and it is normally reached by rappelling off the tooth rather than by walking to it; that rappel is the proof, because the crest between South Twin and Skookum does not simply go on foot. The rock is the second confirmation: the whole ridge here is reddish-orange olivine, coarse and startlingly grippy, and the ridge above the notch climbs on small positive edges with big air on both sides. If you are still down in the green, stream-fed Green Creek Cirque looking up at slabs, you have not gained the crest. If the summit in front of you is the high point of the whole range with everything else below it, that is South Twin, not Skookum.

bivy.name: Green Creek cirque dispersed camp
bivy.notes: This basin under the Green Creek glacier is ringed by Skookum, Little Sister and Cinderella and sits directly below the south end of the traverse, which makes it the natural base for all three of those summits and for the circuit that links them to South Twin. It is reached by branching off the Elbow Lake trail at a switchback onto a blazed climbers path, then working up into the cirque. There are no developed campsites; parties use sandy patches beneath protecting boulders and small flat spots in the heather, and the area holds a wilderness feel that low impact camping is the only way to keep. The springs here are worth planning around, because once you are on the crest above there is nothing. Getting into the basin involves a long loose talus slope where most of what you stand on moves, which is slow and hazardous when wet. Midsummer through early autumn; early season snow makes the approach faster but the river crossing more dangerous.
bivy.water: Two springs of running water in the basin, plus Green Creek lower down. The most dependable water anywhere on the southeast side of the range and the reason this basin is used at all
bivy.permit: National forest, largely within the wilderness unit. Dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve, no developed sites and no facilities. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed at the trailhead. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer. Access from this side does not cross the private timberland, but it does require fording the Middle Fork Nooksack, and the roads serving the trailhead have their own closures.
bivy.capacity: Small dispersed sites, sandy patches under boulders; two or three parties spread out

earlier_research.evidence: A 2017 trip report gives 15 mi round trip and ~7 mi from the trailhead to the base of Old Snowy on the PCT; a mapped track gives 15.5 mi round trip. WTA puts the PCT junction at ~4.7 mi and Oregon Hikers has 1.8 mi more on the PCT to the rocky saddle, plus ~0.5 mi of spur. That is ~7-7.5 mi one way, agreeing with the summit waypoint (7.6) and the 15.5 mi round-trip figure in the same sentence. dist_km (8.5 mi) and itinerary miles (14 RT) are within the measured spread and left alone.

earlier_research.evidence: WTA's route description calls it 'an unmarked junction' where the way goes right through boulders to Old Snowy. Oregon Hikers' Old Snowy page says to follow the ridge south 'on a small unsigned trail'. A 2017 trip report says the path was unmarked but clearly visible. Only SummitPost reports a sign 'as of 2013', which the later sources do not bear out; the row's own navigation finding and approach already say unmarked.

earlier_research.evidence: Two sources put the spur's start at the PCT's crest (~7,600-7,650 ft, its Washington high point), supporting pitch_detail and crowds. But WTA describes a lower unmarked split (right through boulders to Old Snowy, left toward Elk Pass) and another description puts a junction at 7,190 ft; the waypoint[4] pin itself sits at ~7,075 ft on the USGS 1 m DEM and its note (pack stash) matches the upper point. The row appears to conflate two junctions; waypoint elev not changed without resolving which point the pin represents.

earlier_research.evidence: Neither version is confirmed. Oregon Hikers says follow the PCT to its ~7,650 ft crest, then follow the ridge SOUTH on a small trail to the summit; a 2017 trip report calls the final stretch a scramble up Old Snowy's NORTH ridge. That contradicts both the 'south-ridge saddle' (approach, climbing_route, route name) and the itinerary's Old Snowy-Ives col (Ives lies to the south-southeast). Needs owner review of the whole route geometry rather than a one-field patch.

The two sources found put the standard summit path on the ridge NORTH of the summit (walked southward from the PCT crest; the PCT runs on the peak's west slopes), which supports aspect NW / face 'Northwest shoulder' and contradicts the route name 'South Ridge' and beta's 'south side'. The name cannot be changed here and the south-ridge claim runs through approach, climbing_route and approach_variants, so this is flagged rather than patched.

No source clearly says whether the summit route itself crosses Packwood Glacier ice or only its lingering snowfield, so neither the obj_haz/detailed_rack wording nor the crevasses panel was changed.

earlier_research.evidence: A 2017 trip report says the PCT reaches Old Snowy's northwest ridge, splits, and the alternate climbs the ridge to the PCT's Washington high point near 7,600 ft, from which an unmarked path leads south along the ridge (the north ridge) to the summit. A hiking field guide independently says to follow the PCT to its ~7,650 ft crest and then follow the top of the ridge south on an unsigned trail. earlier_research.evidence: A 2017 trip report says that at the northwest ridge the PCT splits, the main PCT traversing Old Snowy's north slopes above and on the Packwood Glacier while the alternate climbs the ridge toward the summit path. A hiking forum thread independently advises that a party wanting to avoid the Packwood crossing can take the trail uphill toward Old Snowy instead, and a PCT section guide calls the alternate the access trail for the Old Snowy summit, running above the regular trail with its glacier patch. The approach, approach variant and descent already say this; only the two waypoint notes were wrong.

Published figures disagree: one route page gives about 14 miles round trip with ~3,600 ft; a GPS-recorded day gives 15 miles/3,500 ft; a mapping app lists 15.5 miles. The hike description's segments (PCT at 4.7 mi, then ~1.8 mi on the PCT and ~0.5 mi of climbers' path) sum to ~7 mi one way (~14 RT), but no two independent sources state the same total. A measured track from trailhead to summit would settle it.

No outside source found that states a car-to-car descent figure for this route; published figures give only gain (3,100-3,800 ft depending on trailhead and source). Per the loss_ft rule it cannot be set from the out-and-back assumption. A source stating total descent for the Snowgrass-Old Snowy round trip would settle it.

row.overview: Old Snowy Mountain sits on the Goat Rocks volcanic crest immediately next to the Pacific Crest Trail, at its highest point in Washington. It's one of the most accessible Goat Rocks summits precisely because the PCT does most of the elevation work: from Snowgrass Flats the trail climbs to an unsigned spur that leaves the PCT and switchbacks up scree and snow to a short, loose, mildly exposed Class 2-3 scramble at the top. The small McCall Glacier lies on the east face and a distinctive natural rock arch (~20 ft) stands near the summit. Old Snowy is frequently combined with a traverse to nearby Ives Peak.
row.beta: From the Snowgrass Flats trailhead, hike ~4.7 miles through forest and meadows to the PCT, then follow the PCT north/west around the mountain's flank to its high point. Leave the PCT on an unsigned boot path that switchbacks up scree/talus to the northwest ridge and follows it south to the summit; the last ~50 feet is loose Class 2–3 rock with real but manageable exposure. An alternate line gains the col between Old Snowy and Ives Peak and follows the ridge crest/just-south-of-crest to the top.
row.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time before starting and stick to it — the exposed ridge and loose summit block are meaningfully more hazardous in afternoon thunderstorms, high wind, or when early-season snow is present, and the long trail approach means a late retreat can mean hiking out in the dark.

row.detailed_rack: No rack is needed — this is an unroped scramble. Trekking poles are widely used and typically stashed just below the final scramble; in early season (persistent snow on the PCT sidehill traverse and the climb up to the summit path) an ice axe and microspikes/traction devices are commonly carried for self-arrest and secure footing.
pro_tips: Many parties combine Old Snowy with Ives Peak as a one-day traverse (mostly Class 2, a few Class 3 moves); start from Old Snowy first to avoid climbing the looser scree slope below Ives
Fill water at Snowgrass Flats/Goat Lake before heading up onto the PCT — there is none higher on the route
Aim for an early summit to beat typical July-August afternoon thunderstorm buildup over the crest
watch_out: The summit spur trail is unsigned and easy to lose in poor visibility — don't wander off the PCT onto random scree
Blocks near the summit are loose underfoot; test holds before weighting them
The natural rock arch near the summit is a scenic landmark but the ground around it is loose and exposed — watch footing while photographing it
row.pro_needs: No technical protection is used on the standard route — it is a trail hike to a Class 2–3 scramble finish. Trekking poles are commonly carried for the snowfields and loose talus.
row.best_season: The PCT traverse below Old Snowy holds a persistent snowfield that is often the last big patch to melt out on the WA PCT's Washington crest, lingering into July in an average year and later in a heavy-snow year — carry an axe even in mid-summer if in doubt. Driest talus and the most stable weather windows are typically August into September, before the first fall storms (which have arrived as early as late September in some years). The FR-21/FR-2150 access road and Snowgrass Flats trail itself often hold snow into June, so early-season attempts should expect a full snow approach, not just a summit snowfield.
row.approach: From the Snowgrass Flats Trailhead (end of FR-2150, elev. ~4,600 ft), start on Trail 96 (Snowgrass Flat Trail). The first stretch climbs gently through forest for roughly 2 miles to a junction with the old Bypass Trail/Trail 96A (stay right on 96 for the more direct, less eroded line). Around 2.4-2.6 miles in you'll hear and then reach the springs that form the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right - the last reliable, easy water source before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek itself; there's no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except during heavy snowmelt, when it can run fast enough to require care. Just beyond the ford (~3.9-4 miles, ~6,400 ft) the trail breaks out of forest into the open heather meadows and wildflower bogs of Snowgrass Flat, a scenic rest and water-filter stop before the climb — note that camping is prohibited within Snowgrass Flat itself under Gifford Pinchot wilderness regulations (36 CFR 261.58(e)); parties camp instead at designated sites above/below the flats. Continue past the Trail 97 junction (west to Cispus Basin/PCT) and the Trail 86 junction (Goat Lake), staying on the main track as it climbs in long benches with Mount Adams and the Goat Rocks opening up behind you. At about 4.7 miles the trail meets the Pacific Crest Trail at roughly 7,100 ft; turn right (north) onto the PCT. Follow the PCT north for about 1.8 miles, traversing rocky, increasingly exposed sidehill terrain on Old Snowy's west flank - snow patches can linger here into midsummer and may require an ice axe/traction for a secure traverse in early season. Watch for an unmarked climbers' path branching right (east) off the PCT toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's northwest ridge; take it and switchback steeply uphill for about a half mile. Many parties stash poles here for the final scramble: the last few hundred feet to the 7,880 ft summit are Class 2-3 hand-and-foot scrambling on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rockfall kicked down by parties above are the main hazard on this final pitch, so avoid stacking directly below other climbers. Total one-way distance is approximately 7.5 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain; round trip is roughly 15.5 miles, typically taking 8.5-9.5 hours car to car.
row.descent_text: This is a walk-off, not a technical descent - there is no rappelling on the standard South Ridge/PCT route. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the Class 2-3 scramble off the summit block (the loose scree and blocky talus here is the descent crux - go slow, test holds, and stay alert for rock knocked loose by parties above or below you), then pick up the climbers' path back down to the PCT. From the PCT junction, follow the trail back south, again watching footing on any lingering snowfields on the exposed sidehill traverse below the ridge (these are firmest and safest to cross in the morning before they soften). Continue south on the PCT to the Trail 96 junction (~7,100 ft) and descend Trail 96 the way you came - back through Snowgrass Flat, across the Snowgrass Creek ford, past the spring/water source, and down through forest to the Snowgrass Flats Trailhead. No ropes, anchors, or rappel gear are needed for this route under normal summer conditions; a rope and basic glacier/snow travel gear are only warranted for early-season attempts with significant snow cover on the PCT traverse or summit scramble.
row.bail: The route is entirely on/near the PCT until the final scramble; retreat at any point is simply reversing the boot path to the PCT and walking the PCT/Trail #96 back to the trailhead. There is no technical descent required to bail from the summit block.

climate.typical: Cool, dry, wind-exposed high-Cascade-crest climate. Summer days are pleasant (60s-70s°F) but the ridge is fully exposed to wind, and afternoon thunderstorms are a real risk. Nights are near or below freezing even in August, and snow is possible in any month at this elevation.

bySeason.fall: Often calm and clear into early October in dry years, but the first snow can arrive by late September; expect short days and freezing nights.
bySeason.spring: Road and trail access to Snowgrass Flats is typically snowed in into June; above that, Old Snowy is essentially a full snow climb requiring axe and likely crampons.
bySeason.summer: Prime season, July through September; the PCT snowfield just below Old Snowy is usually the last big patch on this stretch to melt out and can linger into July.
bySeason.winter: Effectively inaccessible — FR-21/2150 gated and snowed in, and the peak becomes a full winter mountaineering objective on already loose, avalanche-prone terrain.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable throughout the Goat Rocks Wilderness — don't count on a signal even from the summit. Because the peak straddles the Lewis/Yakima county line, give precise location details (landmarks, GPS if available) when calling for help.

approach_variants.notes:
From the Snowgrass Flats trailhead at about 4,600 ft at the end of the forest road, start on Trail 96. It climbs gently through forest roughly 2 miles to a junction with the old bypass trail — stay right on 96 for the more direct, less eroded line.

Around 2.4 to 2.6 miles you reach the springs at the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right, the last easy water before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek; there is no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except in heavy snowmelt.

Just beyond the ford at about 3.9-4 miles and 6,400 ft the trail breaks into the open heather meadows of Snowgrass Flat. Camping is prohibited within the flat itself under wilderness regulations; parties camp at designated sites above or below it.

Continue past the two trail junctions to the PCT at roughly 7,100 ft and turn right, north. Follow the PCT about 1.8 miles across rocky, increasingly exposed sidehill on Old Snowy's west flank.

Round trip is roughly 15.5 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain, typically 8.5 to 9.5 hours car to car. The access road has taken washout damage in past winters, so confirm before driving.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TURN OFF THE PCT IS UNMARKED, AND IT IS THE ONLY THING ON THIS ROUTE YOU CAN GET WRONG.

THE TEST THAT WORKS IN FOG IS ABOUT MOTION, NOT LANDMARKS: the PCT here is SIDEHILLING — traversing across the slope. The climbers' path is THE FIRST THING THAT TURNS UPHILL AND STOPS CONTOURING, branching right, east, toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's northwest ridge. Take the first thing that climbs.

THE NEGATIVE IS EQUALLY MECHANICAL: IF THE PCT STARTS DESCENDING ON THE FAR SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN, YOU HAVE WALKED PAST THE TURN. Go back; do not climb straight up from where you noticed.

DISTANCE CROSS-CHECK: about 1.8 miles north of the Trail 96 junction at 7,100 ft, and the path switchbacks steeply for about half a mile from where you leave the trail.

SECOND MARKER, AND IT SITS BEFORE THE TURN RATHER THAN AFTER IT: a persistent SNOWFIELD on the PCT below the summit lingers into July and is a well-documented trouble spot on the exposed sidehill traverse. Meeting it means the turn is still ahead of you. It is firmest and safest crossed in the morning.

A SOFT CONFIRMATION AT THE SADDLE, WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT IS VISIBLE FROM A DISTANCE: many parties stash trekking poles there for the scramble. A cache of poles on a rocky saddle is a good sign you are at the right one.

BASE OF THE SCRAMBLE: the last few hundred feet to the summit is Class 2-3 hands-and-feet on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rock knocked down by parties above is the hazard, so do not stack directly below other climbers.

AND A NEGATIVE THAT IS ABOUT VISIBILITY RATHER THAN GROUND: once you leave the PCT there is no maintained tread. Poor visibility is the recorded route-finding difficulty on this peak, and the honest response is to turn round at the PCT rather than to search for the spur.

climbing_route.label: Climbers' path to the northwest-ridge saddle
climbing_route.notes: Watch for an unmarked climbers' path branching right (east) off the PCT toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's northwest ridge; take it and switchback steeply uphill for about a half mile. Many parties stash poles here for the final scramble.

climbing_route.label: Final few hundred feet to the 7,880 ft summit
climbing_route.notes: The last few hundred feet are Class 2-3 hand-and-foot scrambling on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rockfall kicked down by parties above are the main hazard on this final pitch, so avoid stacking directly below other climbers.

bivy.name: Snowgrass Flat area backcountry camps
bivy.notes: The standard base for Old Snowy and Ives Peak, and for the West Route on Gilbert. The name misleads: the flat proper is a closed meadow and the legal camping is in the timber and on the benches a little below it, around 6,000 to 6,300 feet, roughly three to four miles from the road. From here Old Snowy is a walk-up on a spur off the crest, Ives is a scree-and-ridge scramble off the col between the two, and Gilbert is a long committing day traversing goat ledges across Cispus Basin at 7,400 to 7,600 feet before the southwest slope. This is the most heavily used corner of the wilderness and the parking fills on weekdays, so arriving Friday evening for a Saturday climb is a poor plan. The meadows hold snow into July in a normal year, which is pleasant for the scrambles and awkward for finding a dry pitch.
bivy.water: Goat Creek and its tributaries run through the basin and are reliable well into the season; treat everything
bivy.permit: Goat Rocks Wilderness permit, free and self-issued from the box at the trailhead — no reservation and no fee. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at Berry Patch or the Snowgrass trailhead. CAMPING WITHIN SNOWGRASS FLAT ITSELF IS PROHIBITED, along with camping within 100 feet of the Pacific Crest Trail and within 100 feet of any lake. Camp only in pre-existing sites.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites in the timber and benches below and around the meadow; no quota and no numbered pads, so capacity is whatever the pre-existing sites hold, and on summer weekends that is fully subscribed

bivy.name: Goat Lake basin
bivy.notes: The other basin camp on this side, reached by the loop that swings north from the Snowgrass trail, and a reasonable alternative when the Snowgrass sites are taken. It sits under Old Snowy's western flank and is slightly further from the crest than Snowgrass, which costs you distance on a summit morning but buys a quieter night. The basin is a cirque and holds snow late, so early-season parties frequently find the lake iced and the campsites buried — the trade for a genuinely alpine setting. Vegetation here is fragile and slow-growing, which is why the existing sites are the only acceptable ones.
bivy.water: The lake, plus outlet streams; the lake can stay partly frozen into midsummer, in which case take water from the outlet
bivy.permit: Same free self-issued wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass as the rest of this trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED within a quarter mile of the lake shore, so bring a stove and do not plan on a fire. The 100-foot setback from lakes applies here and is actively enforced by the condition of the ground.
bivy.capacity: A modest number of established sites scattered back from the shore; the closest ground to the water is off limits, which cuts the usable count sharply

bivy.name: Chambers Lake Campground
bivy.notes: The obvious drive-in base for the Goat Rocks crest, under a mile from both the Berry Patch and Snowgrass trailheads, so you can sleep at the car and be walking at first light without the four-mile carry to Snowgrass. That makes it the right choice for a car-to-car attempt on Old Snowy, and a sensible staging night before shouldering a pack for Ives or Gilbert. It is heavily timbered and low, so there is no view and no acclimatisation value, and the approach roads are long gravel with washboard — allow more driving time than the mileage suggests. Snow closes the access road well into spring, which is the practical limit on early-season attempts from this side.
bivy.water: No potable water on site — bring your own or filter from the lake. Vault toilets are provided
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed for the campground itself, since it sits outside the boundary. A modest per-night fee has been charged in some seasons and waived in others, so carry cash and check the board on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is still required at Berry Patch and the Snowgrass trailhead a short distance up the road.
bivy.capacity: A small forested campground with basic single and double sites; first come, first served

bivy.name: Dana Yelverton Shelter site
bivy.notes: A named point on the crest just below Old Snowy, where a stone shelter once stood and where a hiker died in a summer blizzard in the early 1960s. The shelter is now a scatter of rubble and offers no protection whatsoever, so treat the name as a map label rather than a resource. Its value is position: it is the highest place on this side you can legally sleep, which shortens a summit morning on Old Snowy to almost nothing and puts Ives within an easy pre-dawn traverse. The cost is that it is fully exposed at the high point of the Pacific Crest Trail in Washington, with no water, no wind shelter and no retreat that is not a long descent. The history is the warning: weather arrives here fast and out of season.
bivy.water: None. Snow patches persist nearby into midsummer and can be melted, but from late summer this is a dry camp and water must be carried up from the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issued Goat Rocks Wilderness permit. CAMPFIRES ARE SPECIFICALLY PROHIBITED at this location by wilderness regulation, and the 100-foot setback from the Pacific Crest Trail applies — the trail passes right through, so a legal pitch here takes some walking.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small tents on the crest at best; there is no shelter left to sleep in and the ground is broken rock

name: Standard Route (Northeast summit via Crystal Pass)
prior_findings: Name says 'via Crystal Pass', but every content field describes a different approach.

earlier_research.fact: Which line the route climbs (South Gully/East Ridge vs Crystal Pass/north ridge)
earlier_research.correct_value: The standard route on Inner Constance is the Southeast Couloir–South Defile–South Gully–East Ridge line (Route 2A) from Lake Constance via Avalanche Canyon; the Crystal Pass / north-ridge traverse text belongs to a different line.
earlier_research.evidence: A detailed trip report climbs Inner Constance by the Southeast Couloir–South Defile–South Gully–East Ridge (Route 2A) from Lake Constance, gaining the East Ridge notch from the gully and finishing with a Class 2-3 scramble on pillow basalt. A WTA trip report (2004, 'Lake Constance, Inner Constance') describes the same gully with a discontinuous snow finger, deep moats and a refrigerator-size snow block, reached from Lake Constance. Accounts of Crystal Pass tie it to Mount Constance's West Arete, not Inner Constance. The route name still says 'via Crystal Pass' — names are out of scope for these patches and should be reviewed separately.

earlier_research.correct_value: Reverse the South Gully–East Ridge line to Avalanche Canyon and Lake Constance, then out the Lake Constance path and the Dosewallips Road.
earlier_research.evidence: The trip report for the South Gully–East Ridge route descends the same line and calls it an excellent descent route with adequate snow, glissading the lower couloir; the WTA 2004 report describes down-climbing the gully and defile, staying in the moats and down-climbing rock steps. descent_text (the longer field, the one shown) described a Crystal Pass / Constance Pass exit and is rewritten to match `descent`.

earlier_research.evidence: The NPS Lake Constance Route page describes the approach from the Dosewallips Road washout (~700 ft) and a very steep climb to the lake at 4,800 ft; WTA's Lake Constance guide gives the lake at 4,800 ft, 2.2 mi one way from the trailhead, above the washed-out road. The Route 2A trip report bikes the road, hikes to Lake Constance and goes up Avalanche Canyon. The approach paragraph, itinerary day 1, its timing note, and partner requirements are rewritten to this approach; the Crystal Pass way stays as the second approach variant.

earlier_research.correct_value: About 16 miles round trip (~8 mi one way) via Lake Constance; the '16 mi one-way' figure is removed with the Crystal Pass approach text.
earlier_research.evidence: The Route 2A trip report gives 16 miles total (8 by bike, 8 on foot), matching totalNote's 16 mi round trip and dist_km 12.9 (8 mi one way). The '16 mi one-way' statement in the approach belonged to the Crystal Pass way and is gone in the rewritten approach. The per-day mileages (6.5 in, 5 out) still differ and are recorded as a separate open item.

earlier_research.evidence: Day 1 (in) is 6.5 mi and day 3 (out) is 5 mi over the same road and path. No source gives the washout-to-lake distance consistently (NPS and WTA give ~5 mi of road plus ~2 mi of path; the trip report says ~4 mi of road each way). Not patched.

earlier_research.evidence: The Route 2A trip report gives ~7,300 ft gained and lost, matching gain_ft. The itinerary days sum to 6,000 ft and totalNote says 6,000 ft, but no source gives per-day gains, and only one source states the total, so neither the days nor totalNote are changed.

The Route 2A trip report describes Class 3-4 sections in the upper defile/gully and a Class 2-3 scramble on the East Ridge, with no roof or chimney; the 'low 5th' grade, rock_grade 5.0 and the chimney/roof ('cave of despair') in pro_needs appear to come from the Crystal Pass line. Only one source describes the South Gully grade, so grade, rock_grade and pro_needs are not changed.

earlier_research.evidence: The Route 2A trip report recommends early summer for snow cover and found mid-July melt already producing difficult moats and loose rock. On the row, season, best_season, beta ('excellent when snow is firm'), approach_variants[0].season and the South Defile waypoint (moats opening by mid-late season) all favour early-to-mid season; seasonal_guidance is the lone outlier and is brought into line.

earlier_research.evidence: No source found states a commitment grade for this route. The trip report did it in ~10.5 hours of movement; the grade may describe only the climb from camp. Not changed.

earlier_research.fact: Location of the Class 3-4 rock step
earlier_research.correct_value: The rock step is where the gully exits onto the East Ridge at the notch; above it the ridge to the summit is Class 2-3.
earlier_research.evidence: The Route 2A trip report has the steep snow gully leading to the East Ridge notch, followed by a Class 2-3 scramble on pillow basalt to the summit. On the row, pitch_detail[3], the East Ridge Notch waypoint, beta and approach_variants[0].baseFinding all put the step at the notch; the schedule, day-2 note and `descent` (summit block) are the outliers.

earlier_research.correct_value: Pillow basalt, not granite.
earlier_research.evidence: Inner Constance is built of tilted Eocene pillow basalt (Wikipedia geology entry), and the Route 2A trip report describes basaltic rock and pillow basalt on the East Ridge. watch_out's 'granite and metamorphic rock' is wrong.

The NPS Lake Constance Route page recommends early reservations for trips between May 1 and September 30; the NPS wilderness reservations page gives the quota-area summer season as May 15–October 15. The park's two pages disagree, so neither field is changed.

earlier_research.evidence: NPS says the road closure adds about 6.5 miles to reach the old trailhead; WTA says to hike or bike 5+ miles of road above the washout. With the Lake Constance turn-off ~5 mi up (waypoint), '5.5 miles past the turn-off' cannot also be 6.5 mi from the gate. The wrong clause is removed and the 6.5-mile total kept.

earlier_research.correct_value: Vehicle traffic ends and parking is at the washout, about 8.5 miles from US-101.
earlier_research.evidence: WTA's Lake Constance guide says to drive 8.5 miles to the washout where vehicle traffic ends, then hike or bike above it; NPS says hikers start at the washout (~700 ft); the Route 2A trip report starts at the road gate at the washout. road.status's 'washout is roughly a mile farther up' is wrong.

earlier_research.evidence: The WTA hike page gives 5+ miles of closed road above the washout plus a 4.4-mile round-trip path (about 2.2 mi each way), and the NPS route page gives about 5 miles of road plus ~1.8-2 mi of path; both put the lake about 7 mi one way, matching the Lake Constance pin (7.2 mi) but neither day 1 (6.5) nor day 3 (5). Fixing both days would push the itinerary total to ~18 mi and contradict the totalNote's 16 mi round trip, which the one trip report (16 mi RT to the summit) supports. Settling needs a second measured car-to-summit round-trip distance to fix the total, then days 1 and 3 can be set equal.

Only one trip report states a car-to-car figure for this route (~7,300 ft gained and lost), matching gain_ft; no second source stating the total or per-day gains for Route 2A was found in further searches (summitpost, cascadeclimbers, WTA and other trip reports cover Mount Constance, not Inner Constance). Itinerary days (6,000 ft) and totalNote remain unchanged; a second trip report stating the total would settle the totalNote.

The one detailed Route 2A trip report describes a Class 3-4 exit step and Class 2-3 scrambling on the East Ridge, with no chimney or roof; a second party's report of an Inner Constance attempt names routes 2, 2A and 3 but gives no grades, and Wikipedia gives only the FA. No second source grading the South Gully-East Ridge line was found, so grade, rock_grade and pro_needs are unchanged; a guidebook-independent second report grading Route 2A would settle it.

earlier_research.evidence: No source found states a commitment grade for Inner Constance Route 2A; Wikipedia and the trip reports give no grade. The one trip report did it in about 10.5 hours of movement. A published commitment grade for the route would settle it.

earlier_research.evidence: The NPS wilderness reservations page and the Recreation.gov Olympic Wilderness permit page both state the summer reservation season is May 15 through October 15 (released April 15), and Recreation.gov lists Lake Constance among the reservable quota areas; a third-party permit guide repeats May 15-Oct 15. The NPS Lake Constance route page's May 1-Sept 30 is only a window for which early reservations are recommended. One secondary blog claims a June 15-Oct 15 Lake Constance season, so the waypoint states the quota without dates and access.permit keeps the season.

earlier_research.evidence: A detailed trip report for Inner Constance describes the Lake Constance - Avalanche Canyon - South Defile - South Gully - East Ridge line and does not go via Crystal Pass, and every content field of the row agrees. The watch_out 'Crystal Pass crossing' line fits the row's alternative approach over Crystal Pass and is left alone.

A second report describing the East Ridge rock would settle it.

earlier_research.evidence: Two hiking guides say to drive 8.5 miles up Dosewallips Road from US-101 to the vehicle road end. One of them puts the old washout about 1 mile beyond it, and the other puts a washout about 1.2 mi beyond. A news report puts the washout itself at about 10 miles from US-101, which is the source of the stale 10.5 figure but is not where cars park. So the waypoint's ~9 mi was nearer, and 10.5 mi to the parking is wrong.

row.name: Standard Route (Northeast summit via Crystal Pass)
row.fa: Unknown; first ascent of peak 1939 by David Harrah party
row.season: Jun-Sep (snow-dependent; best attempted early-to-mid season while the couloir/defile still holds snow bridging the moats)
hazards: Notoriously loose, rotten Olympic pillow basalt with constant rockfall on warm days
Exposed roped climbing including a steep, committing chimney/roof section ('cave of despair' in trip reports)
Easy to be drawn onto the wrong (southwest) summit, which has no easy access to the true northeast high point
Steep snowfields and a small glacier high on the route early season
Deep moats bordering the snow finger in the South Gully/defile, requiring repeated stemming between snow and rock to bypass
Collapsing or sliding snow blocks in the gully as the day warms — a documented incident involved a refrigerator-size block breaking loose and striking a climber
row.overview: Inner Constance (7,672 ft by LiDAR) is the fifth-highest summit in the Olympic Mountains, a rugged pyramid just west of Mount Constance (its line parent, 0.9 mi east) across the glacially carved Avalanche Canyon, within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park. The mountain is built of Eocene tilted pillow basalt, rotten and loose throughout. David Harrah's party is credited with the first ascent in 1939. The commonly described standard line climbs out of Avalanche Canyon via a South Gully/snow-filled defile to the East Ridge ('Route 2A') rather than via nearby Crystal Pass, which is a separate saddle/viewpoint climbers sometimes visit instead when they bail on the summit. Climbers occasionally report uncertainty about whether they've reached the true high point versus a nearby sub-summit in the Olympics' notorious cloud cover.
row.beta: From Lake Constance, ascend Avalanche Canyon on climber paths and snow patches to a broad couloir below The Thumb landmark. Ascend the broad couloir on firm snow, veering right into a steeper secondary couloir. Follow a narrow, snow-filled defile on the right side, featuring a hard snow finger with moats. At higher elevations, climb a steep snow gully with discontinuous snow finger, stemming out to rock and scrambling up the moat. Gain the east ridge crest via a final pitch of Class 3 rock, then follow Class 2-3 scrambling on solid pillow basalt to the summit. Route 2A is described as excellent when snow is firm; when snow melts in late summer, the underlying scree becomes unpleasantly loose.
row.turnaround: Turn around if: (1) snow conditions in the defile/gully become unsafe with excessive rockfall or avalanche debris; (2) you are not at the east ridge crest by mid-afternoon, as darkness will prevent safe scrambling; (3) weather deteriorates with heavy precipitation or lightning risk; (4) any team member shows signs of altitude sickness, exhaustion, or inability to move safely.
row.face: South Gully and East Ridge, above Avalanche Canyon
row.permit: Olympic National Park: no permit for day climbs; all overnight wilderness stays require a wilderness camping permit via Recreation.gov.
row.comms: Cell service is unreliable in the canyon and at higher elevations of Olympic National Park. Satellite messengers (InReach, Garmin) are recommended for emergency communication. The Dosewallips River drainage receives poor to no cellular coverage.
row.descent: Reverse the South Gully–East Ridge line: scramble back down the East Ridge, down-climb/rappel the Class 3-4 rock step at the notch, then descend the snow finger through the gully, staying alert for moats on both sides and for wet-day rockfall/collapsing snow blocks (a documented near-miss involved a refrigerator-size block of sliding snow). Published descriptions note this line (Route 2A) as a workable descent option back to Avalanche Canyon and Lake Constance.

waypoints.name: Dosewallips Road washout parking (FR-2610)
waypoints.note: Vehicle-accessible road end at the 2002 washout (~8.5 mi from Hwy 101); self-issue wilderness permit kiosk here before biking/hiking the closed roadbed.
waypoints.directions: Drive Dosewallips Road inland from US-101, roughly 8.5 miles, to the vehicle-accessible road end at the 2002 washout. Fill in a self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk before starting up the closed roadbed.

waypoints.name: Lake Constance Trailhead
waypoints.note: Unmaintained climbers' path splits off the old Dosewallips roadbed and climbs steeply up the narrow Constance Creek canyon; unsigned and easy to walk past.
waypoints.directions: The road beyond has been closed to motor vehicles since the 2002 flood but stays open to foot and bicycle, and most parties ride it; a short riverside bypass gets around the washed-out section before the old roadbed resumes. About 5 miles up, an unmaintained climbers' path splits off the roadbed and starts up the narrow Constance Creek canyon. It is unsigned and easy to walk straight past, so watch for it.

waypoints.name: Creekside Camp Bench
waypoints.note: Trail briefly levels crossing the valley floor beside Constance Creek; flat spot with an established fire ring and reliable running water, a common rest/camp break before the final steep push.
waypoints.directions: The climbers' path climbs steeply and directly up the canyon, unmaintained and choked with blowdown, and this lower section is the hardest walking of the trip. At around 3,100 ft the tread briefly levels out on the valley floor beside Constance Creek at a flat bench with an established fire ring and reliable running water.

waypoints.name: Lake Constance
waypoints.note: Emerald backcountry lake cupped in a rock bowl at the mouth of Avalanche Canyon; camping permits are quota-limited, so use existing sites to protect the fragile basin.
waypoints.directions: From the bench the path resumes its steep push, gaining the last 1,700 ft to the lake at 4,800 ft, cupped in a rock bowl at the mouth of Avalanche Canyon. Camping is quota-limited, so use the existing sites.

waypoints.name: Avalanche Canyon / The Thumb
waypoints.note: Barren, rocky Avalanche Canyon opens north from the lake, a stark contrast to the rainforest below; the Thumb rock formation marks where the South Chute (Mount Constance) and South Gully (Inner Constance) lines diverge on faint, intermittent climbers' track.
waypoints.directions: Head north out of the lake basin into Avalanche Canyon, barren and rocky in contrast to the rainforest below, on faint and intermittent climbers' track and snow patches. Continue up-canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb, the rock formation that marks where the South Chute on Mount Constance and the South Gully on Inner Constance diverge.

waypoints.name: South Defile Snow Choke
waypoints.note: Snow-filled defile narrows to a roughly 2-ft gap with 5-10 ft deep moats opening on each side by mid-late season; parties have reported refrigerator-size snow blocks calving here, so move through quickly and probe snow bridges before committing.
waypoints.directions: From the mouth of the canyon follow the faint, intermittent climbers' track and snow patches north up Avalanche Canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb, then take the Inner Constance branch and veer right into a steeper secondary couloir that narrows into the defile. Snow blocks calve out of this constriction as the day warms, so move through it quickly and probe the bridges over the moats before committing weight to them.

waypoints.name: East Ridge Notch
waypoints.note: A steep, discontinuous snow finger tops out at this notch on Inner Constance's East Ridge; a short Class 3 rock step gains the ridge crest before the summit scramble.
waypoints.directions: Above the defile the gully continues on discontinuous snow, with repeated stemming between the snow finger and the rock walls to get around the moats and a few short up- and downclimbs on rock where the snow runs out. A steep snow finger tops out at the notch; exit the gully onto the crest by way of a short Class 3-4 rock step.

waypoints.name: Inner Constance
waypoints.note: True summit (7,672 ft), the Olympics' 4th/5th-highest peak; final approach is fun Class 2-3 scrambling on pillow basalt along the East Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow the East Ridge crest from the notch on Class 2-3 scrambling over pillow basalt to the top. Rock across this massif is notoriously rotten, so keep the party tight and out of each other's fall line. Do not let the line pull you toward the southwest summit — it has no easy connection across to the true northeast high point.

sectionBreakdown.note: From the Dosewallips Road washout, bike or walk the closed road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' path, then climb it steeply to camp at Lake Constance.
An alpine start on firm snow up a broad couloir into a narrow, moat-lined snow defile, then a steep discontinuous snow finger gaining the East Ridge. From the ridge it's a Class 2-…
Break camp and reverse the approach, dropping back down toward the Dosewallips River trail and out to the trailhead (or bike cache, given the road washout closure). Mostly downhill…

row.detailed_rack: A rope and a light-to-moderate alpine rack (nuts, small-to-mid cams, slings) for the exposed low-5th-class pitches; ice axe and possibly crampons for the snowfield/small glacier depending on conditions.
pro_tips: Navigate carefully to the northeast summit — the southwest point is a dead end.
Move early to avoid afternoon rockfall on the snowfield.
Treat every hold as suspect and helmet up for the whole upper route.
row.watch_out:
Rotten rock and rockfall hazard throughout upper peak—pillow basalt severely weathered; continuous hazard from loosening rocks; stay alert and compact; helmet mandatory
Exposed chimney/roof pitch on upper pitches—significant protection challenge on friable rock; runout potential if placements fail; requires confident climbing and careful anchor placement
Navigation to correct NE summit complicated by multiple peaks—wrong summit selection can add hours and difficulty; study photos and use GPS; false summits create fatigue and disorientation
Steep snow and small glacier high on route—transition from rock to snow/ice can be hazardous; assess conditions and have appropriate tools (ice axe, crampons); late season bare ice or crevasse exposure
Crystal Pass crossing—bergschrund potential; late season route-finding confusion; always probe and belay uncertain snow/ice crossings
Altitude exposure with sustained climbing—7700+ feet with continuous elevation gain; altitude sickness possible; acclimatization and hydration essential
Weather exposure on open ridge traverse—afternoon storms common in Olympics; exposed position dangerous with lightning; start pre-dawn
Descent terrain equally demanding—route-finding on descent must-do; darkness increases risk; maintain focus on descent line throughout climb
row.pro_needs: Protection for several exposed Class 4 / low-5th-class pitches on poor rock, including the steep chimney/roof move below the summit.
row.best_season: Late June through July is favored while the South Gully/defile still holds consolidated snow, which makes the ascent line far more secure; by August the snow largely melts out and the same gully becomes unpleasantly loose rock and scree (per first-hand trip reports), still climbable but harder and looser. The approach trail to Lake Constance is generally passable from late June into September.
row.approach: From the Dosewallips River Road washout (~700 ft) — the road has been closed to motor vehicles since a 2002 flood but stays open to foot and bicycle travel — most parties bike the closed roadbed, getting around the washed-out section on a riverside bypass. Several miles up, an unsigned, unmaintained climbers' path leaves the roadbed and climbs very steeply up the narrow Constance Creek canyon: roughly 3,300 ft in about 2 miles, choked with blowdown in its lower part and with some hands-on scrambling higher up, past a small creekside bench near 3,100 ft, to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft, the usual camp (a wilderness permit is needed and the lake is a quota area). From the lake, head north into barren Avalanche Canyon on a faint, intermittent climbers' track and snow patches to the broad couloir below the Thumb, where the South Chute of Mount Constance and the South Gully of Inner Constance part ways. A much longer alternative follows the closed road to its old end, climbs the Constance Pass Trail and crosses Crystal Pass into the head of Avalanche Canyon; it avoids the Lake Constance path's steep lower section. Expect a 2–3 day trip either way.
row.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: scramble back down the East Ridge to the notch, downclimb or rappel the short rock step into the gully, then descend the discontinuous snow finger and the South Defile, watching for moats on both sides and for snow blocks that loosen as the day warms. Where the snow is firm and runs out safely, the lower couloir can be plunge-stepped or glissaded. Loose rock is a hazard the whole way off the summit, so keep the party close together and out of each other's fall line. From the broad couloir below the Thumb, walk back down Avalanche Canyon to Lake Constance, then descend the steep climbers' path and the closed Dosewallips Road to the washout.
row.bail: Retreat is by rappelling and reversing the route; there is no quick escape. Bail from below the technical climbing if weather or rockfall conditions are poor.

pitch_detail.notes: From Lake Constance, ascend Avalanche Canyon (barren, rocky terrain) toward the base of the route below Crystal Pass and 'The Thumb'.

Broad snow couloir narrows into the South Defile; a roughly 2 ft snow-choked constriction with 5-10 ft moats along the sides -- kick steps up the hard snow finger and stem across moats to reach rock where needed.
Continue up the South Gully above the defile; discontinuous snow again requires moat-crossing maneuvers and some downclimbing/upclimbing on rock.
Exit the gully onto the East Ridge via a short rock step.

Descend by reversing the same line, down-climbing/rappelling the rock step and glissading or plunge-stepping the gully where snow allows.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late June through July, while the South Gully and defile still hold consolidated snow over the moats

July.reason: The best month for this line: snow still fills the defile and bridges the moats, though they widen through the month and a small glacier remnant lingers high on the route early on

June.reason: Late June opens the favoured window while the gully and defile hold consolidated snow; earlier in the month the approach can still be snowbound and the upper snow needs an avalanche check

August.reason: The gully's snow largely melts out, leaving loose rock, scree and deep moats; still climbable but harder and looser than earlier in the season

September.reason: Still within the best-season window, but a short shoulder season where early storms become possible per the climate notes; watch weather windows closely

weather.typical: Eastern Olympic rain-shadow climate keeps this route drier than the west-side Olympics, but weather is fast-changing and the rock stays persistently loose regardless of season
weather.probability: Warm summer days bring afternoon rockfall off sun-loosened rock and snow; by September, early-season storms become a real possibility and can end the climbing window abruptly

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Sustained, serious exposure on the roped chimney/roof pitch and on exposed 4th/low-5th class terrain leading to the correct (northeast) summit; the notoriously rotten Olympic rock means both leader falls and rockfall from other parties carry high consequence, and straying onto the wrong (southwest) summit adds route-finding-related fall exposure on unfamiliar terrain.

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance and Avalanche Canyon to the South Gully
approach_variants.notes:
The shorter of the two ways in, at roughly 8 miles one-way. Bike or walk about 5 miles of closed Dosewallips Road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail at about 1,425 ft, then the steep unmaintained boot path up the narrow Constance Creek canyon. At roughly 3,100 ft the tread briefly levels on the valley floor beside the creek at a flat bench with an established fire ring and running water — a common rest stop. From there the last 1,700 ft to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camping at the lake is quota-limited.

From the lake head north into Avalanche Canyon, barren and rocky in stark contrast to the rainforest below, on faint intermittent climbers' track and snow patches, and continue up-canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and snow-dependent in a way most Olympic scrambles are not — this line wants snow still bridging the moats in the defile, so early to mid season is better than late
hazards: Deep moats on both sides of the snow finger in the South Gully defile, needing repeated stemming to bypass
Collapsing or sliding snow blocks in the constriction as the day warms — a documented injury
Notoriously loose, rotten Olympic pillow basalt with rockfall on warm days
Easy to be drawn onto the southwest summit, which has no easy access to the true northeast high point
Steep snowfields and a small glacier high on the route early season
The Lake Constance trail is one of the steepest and least maintained in the range
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THIS CLIMB IS A FORK, AND THE FORK IS MARKED BY A ROCK FORMATION CALLED THE THUMB. Head up Avalanche Canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb. That is where the South Chute (which belongs to MOUNT Constance) and the South Gully (which belongs to INNER Constance, this route) diverge. Two summits sit above one canyon and the Thumb is the thing that tells the two lines apart.

THE FOG TEST THAT DOES NOT NEED THE THUMB, AND IT IS THE BETTER ONE, IS THE SHAPE OF THE GULLY YOU END UP IN. From the broad couloir, veer RIGHT into a steeper secondary couloir, which narrows into a snow-filled DEFILE. That defile constricts to roughly a two-foot gap with moats five to ten feet deep opening on either side of the snow by mid-to-late season. Nothing else in this canyon does that. If your gully stays broad and open all the way up, you are in the Mount Constance South Chute and climbing the wrong peak.

SECOND TEST, higher: above the defile the snow finger goes discontinuous and you stem repeatedly between snow and rock to get round the moats, with short up- and downclimbs on rock where the snow runs out. A steep finger tops out at a notch on the East Ridge near 7,200 ft, gained by a short Class 3-4 rock step. If you are still on continuous snow with no stemming, you have not reached the defile yet.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE, AND IT IS THE RECORDED WAY THIS ROUTE GOES WRONG: from the East Ridge the line pulls naturally toward the SOUTHWEST summit, which has no easy connection across to the true NORTHEAST high point. Follow the East Ridge crest on Class 2-3 pillow basalt to the northeast top; if the ridge you are on is running away southwest, you are heading for the wrong summit.

SAFETY NOTE THAT IS PART OF THE ROUTE-FINDING: snow blocks calve out of the defile constriction as the day warms — a refrigerator-sized block struck a climber there. Move through it quickly and probe the bridges over the moats before weighting them.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road to Constance Pass, then Crystal Basin and Crystal Pass
approach_variants.notes:
About 16 miles one-way and worth it to some parties precisely because it avoids the Lake Constance trail's brutally steep, unmaintained, blowdown-choked lower section. From the Dosewallips washout at roughly 600 ft, bike or walk the closed roadbed — working round the washout on a riverside bypass — past the Lake Constance turn-off to the old Dosewallips Campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end, about 6.5 miles and 1,900 ft of cumulative gain from the gate.

Pick up the Constance Pass Trail and climb south and southwest through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. The upper stretch is steep open meadow and scree, with the last reliable water at creek crossings below treeline.

From Constance Pass leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin and climb to Crystal Pass, the windswept notch on the Constance-Warrior massif that divides the Dosewallips side from Avalanche Canyon. Expect a two or three day trip with a camp near Constance Pass or in upper Avalanche Canyon.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the snow below Crystal Pass is safe
hazards: The climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass; unmarked talus, scree and snow between there and Constance Pass
Notoriously rotten pillow basalt with constant rockfall on warm days
A steep, committing chimney and roof section high on the peak that trip reports call the cave of despair
Being drawn onto the southwest summit
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM CRYSTAL PASS THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS DIRECTLY BELOW YOU RATHER THAN ABOVE YOU, WHICH IS THE ONE REAL ADVANTAGE OF THIS SIDE. Descend south into upper Avalanche Canyon on the intermittent climbers' path through scree and talus, keeping to the RIGHT (north) side of the canyon, past the Thumb, and then contour and climb toward Inner Constance's northeast side.

THE TEST IS STILL THE THUMB AND THE DEFILE, and it still works from above: the fork you want is the one where the South Gully leaves the broad couloir and veers into a steeper secondary couloir that NARROWS to a two-foot gap with deep moats. Coming from Crystal Pass you can also take the northeast side directly — a short step just above the pass leads into a rising traverse along the RIGHT side of the north ridge crest, broken blocky Class 2-3 with occasional Class 4 and low fifth where the crest steepens.

THE FOG TEST FOR THAT NORTHEAST LINE IS WHICH SIDE OF THE CREST YOU ARE ON. Stay on the crest's RIGHT-hand side as you climb. If you have crossed over and are traversing on the other flank, you are off the line, and the rock over there is worse.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: the same trap as the other variant — the mountain pulls toward the SOUTHWEST summit, which does not connect easily to the true northeast high point. Keep working toward the NORTHEAST top.

HONEST LIMIT: the informal climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and this stretch is talus, scree and early-season snow with real route-finding demands. A rope and axe may be prudent on the snow remnant below the pass early in the year.

climbing_route.label: Avalanche Canyon to the South Defile
climbing_route.notes: From Lake Constance, go north up Avalanche Canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb, then veer right into a steeper secondary couloir that narrows into the moat-lined snow of the South Defile.

climbing_route.label: South Gully to the East Ridge and summit
climbing_route.notes: Above the defile, climb the steep, discontinuous snow finger of the South Gully, stemming between snow and rock around the moats, to the notch on the East Ridge. A short rock step puts you on the crest, and Class 2-3 scrambling on pillow basalt leads along the ridge to the northeast (true) summit.

row.overview: A steep, committing snow/ice headwall on Adams' northeast side, below Roosevelt Cliff, fed by the Wilson Glacier — one of the mountain's most serious and rarely repeated headwall lines, grouped with the neighboring Rusk Glacier Headwall as among the most dangerous routes on the peak. Rockfall is a major hazard on these east-side headwalls, so climbers should only attempt it early season in cold, frozen conditions.
row.beta: Grouped with Victory Ridge and the Rusk Glacier Headwall as among Mount Adams's most challenging and infrequently climbed routes, this line ascends Roosevelt Cliff — a rock rib that splits the Wilson Glacier, named (along with the glacier itself) by Claude Ewing Rusk in 1919. The Wilson Glacier is fed by avalanching snow and ice off the summit ice cap starting around 10,800 ft and descends to a terminus near 7,400 ft on the reservation side of the mountain.
