row.approach: The Wilson Glacier sits on the east side of Mount Adams, descending from around 10,600 ft to a terminus near 7,400 ft — a less-visited, less-documented flank than the standard south or north-side routes. Parties reach it via the Cold Springs/South Climb trailhead (5,600 ft, FS Rd 8040 off FS Rd 80): follow the South Climb Trail #183 about 1 mile up an old road bed to the junction with the Round the Mountain Trail, then instead of continuing north toward Lunch Counter, follow Round the Mountain Trail east below Crescent Glacier onto Yakama Nation land, where a separate tribal permit is required and the trail ends at Hellroaring Canyon; the way on, north around the mountain's eastern flank toward the Wilson/Klickitat glacier basins, is a long off-trail traverse with route-finding, creek crossings, and exposure to rockfall directly below the headwall's cliff bands. Given the route's distance (~27 km) and gain (6,700 ft) roughly match the other long approach routes on this mountain, expect a full day just to reach a camp near the toe of the Wilson Glacier before a summit attempt.
row.descent_text: The descent reverses back down the South Climb to Cold Springs: after topping out via the headwall, parties traverse over toward the summit plateau and descend the standard South Climb route (non-technical snow/scree walk-off, good glissading in early season) back to Lunch Counter and out to the Cold Springs trailhead — a different, easier line than the ascent. This is a walk-off, not a rappel descent. Because the Wilson Glacier Headwall itself is steep snow/ice below cliff bands, a party that needs to bail mid-face rather than finish over the top could reasonably rope down using pickets or V-threads in snow/ice, but this would be an improvised retreat, not a documented standard rappel.
row.bail: Drop back toward the South Climb route if out of condition

approach_variants.name: Cold Springs and the Round the Mountain Trail east around the mountain
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cold Springs and South Climb trailhead at about 5,600 ft at the end of the forest road north of Trout Lake, follow South Climb Trail #183 about a mile up an old road bed to the junction with the Round the Mountain Trail.

Instead of continuing north toward the Lunch Counter, follow the Round the Mountain Trail east and then north, contouring below the Crescent Glacier and around the mountain's eastern flank toward the Wilson and Klickitat glacier basins. This is a long, mostly off-trail traverse with route-finding, creek crossings, and exposure to rockfall directly below the headwall's cliff bands.

The Wilson descends from around 10,600 ft to a terminus near 7,400 ft, and it is split by a rock rib. Expect a full day to reach a camp near its toe before any summit attempt.

This is one of the least-visited and least-documented flanks of the mountain. The descent is not a reversal: parties top out and come down the standard South Climb to Cold Springs.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECISION HAPPENS ABOUT A MILE FROM THE CAR AND IT IS A TURNING, NOT AN ARRIVAL. At the junction of the South Climb Trail with the Round the Mountain Trail, the standard South Spur route goes NORTH toward the Lunch Counter; this route goes EAST. If you are climbing toward the Lunch Counter, you are on the standard South Climb and this route is already behind you.

THAT IS THE ONE ERROR WORTH GUARDING, BECAUSE IT IS RECOVERABLE ONLY BY WALKING BACK DOWN. Everything after it is a long contour.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE BASE IS A GLACIER SPLIT BY A ROCK RIB. The Wilson runs from about 10,600 ft down to about 7,400 ft and a rock rib divides it. A headwall above a glacier that is bisected by a rib is the confirmation. An unbroken glacier with no rib in it is not the Wilson.

THE SECOND POSITIVE IS ASPECT AND IT IS THE COARSEST BUT MOST RELIABLE: you must be on the EAST side of the mountain. Going around the eastern flank is the whole approach. If the sun is rising behind the mountain rather than in front of you, you have not come far enough round.

THE NEGATIVE THAT MATTERS FOR SAFETY RATHER THAN NAVIGATION: the contour runs directly beneath cliff bands that shed rock. It is a place to keep moving. Persistent rockfall on these east-side headwalls is among the reasons most of them remain unrepeated, so a rope-length of comfortable ground is not evidence the ground above you is quiet.

WHAT BEING ON A NEIGHBOURING BASIN LOOKS LIKE: keep going round and you reach the Klickitat basin. The Wilson is the first of the two you meet coming from the south.

bivy.notes: Most South Climb parties sleep here the night before, either to acclimatise a little or to get an alpine start without carrying a camp to the Lunch Counter. Facilities are primitive — a vault toilet, no piped water, no developed fee sites. Access is FR 80 to FR 8040 and then FR 8040-500, roughly eight miles of washboarded and rutted gravel with the last three miles steep, narrow and switchbacked; ordinary cars get up it at low speed but a low-slung vehicle can bottom out, and RVs and trailers should not attempt it. The road generally opens around mid-May and is usually clear of snow by the start of July, so early-season parties should expect to park lower and walk.
bivy.water: Unreliable. Treat this as a dry camp and arrive with water. Small springs and Morrison Creek near the road can be running early in the season and gone by late summer.

row.overview: A twin-summited peak in the Skagit Range of the North Cascades, directly across the Nooksack River valley from Mount Shuksan and just south of Mount Larrabee, within the Mount Baker Wilderness. The standard route follows USFS Trail #673 through old-growth forest and heather meadows to a ridge crest, then continues off-trail up a steep, loose scramblers' path to the false (west, ~6,600 ft) and true (east, 6,891 ft) summits. It's popular both as a strenuous day hike/scramble and as a backpacking or spring ski-touring objective, and is one of the first Baker Highway trails to melt out each year because of its south exposure.
row.beta: This route continues past the West Peak false summit to the higher East Peak (6,891 ft), the mountain's true summit. The maintained trail ends on the shoulder near 5,400-5,600 ft; everything above is unmaintained boot path and open scrambling. The route involves a steep permanent snowfield traverse requiring an ice axe at all times, then a short, relatively straightforward scramble to the top. The route offers commanding views of Mount Baker, Mount Shuksan, Mount Sefrit, and the surrounding North Cascades peaks.
row.turnaround: An early alpine start is essential; any party not reaching the summit ridge by early afternoon should turn around and descend to avoid travel in darkness on steep, exposed terrain. Never traverse the permanent snowfield after 3:00 PM given the additional darkness risk.
row.permit: Free self-issue Mount Baker Wilderness permit or trailhead registration; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
row.comms: Cellular service is unreliable to non-existent in the Mount Baker Wilderness. Satellite messengers (Garmin inReach or similar) are strongly recommended for wilderness areas. The trailhead is approximately 46 miles from Bellingham.
row.descent: Reverse the ascent ridge and trail. The loose, exposed scrambling near the true summit and the steep, unmaintained goat path down to the maintained trail's end are the trickiest sections to downclimb carefully, especially on wet rock or lingering snow; many parties turn around at the easier 6,600 ft false (west) summit rather than continue the exposed ridge to the true 6,891 ft summit.

waypoints.name: Goat Mountain Trailhead
waypoints.note: On FS-32 (Hannegan Pass Rd) 2.1 mi off SR 542; Northwest Forest Pass required, vault toilet and parking on both sides of the road.
waypoints.directions: Reach the trailhead via Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32), off SR 542 near Glacier, about two miles up from the Glacier Public Service Center. Day-use parking is on both sides of the road, with a vault toilet on site, and a Northwest Forest Pass is required.

waypoints.name: Mt. Baker Wilderness Boundary / Old Goat Trail split
waypoints.note: Trail enters the Mt. Baker Wilderness here; an unsigned climbers' path ("Old Goat Trail") splits east toward a former lookout site — stay on the main trail.
waypoints.directions: Goat Mountain Trail #673 climbs steeply and almost without let-up from the trailhead, switchbacking through old-growth fir and hemlock and crossing a small cascading creek several times in the first mile. Around 3,200 ft the grade eases and the tread traverses onto a narrow side-hill ridge. The wilderness boundary sign is on that ridge; just past it an unsigned spur splits east toward an old lookout site, so stay on the main tread.

waypoints.name: 5,200-ft Knob
waypoints.note: Open alpine meadows and huckleberries (in season) around this viewpoint knob, with clear sightlines to Baker, Shuksan, and Sefrit.
waypoints.directions: Keep climbing on maintained trail as forest gives way to heather and huckleberry meadows and the views south to Baker, Shuksan and Sefrit open up. The trail gains the ridge crest at the viewpoint knob.

waypoints.name: End of maintained Trail 673
waypoints.note: Trail 673 officially terminates on the ridge crest at 5,600 ft; beyond here toward the East Peak is an unmaintained, unmarked boot path.
waypoints.directions: Follow the crest a little farther to where the maintained tread officially ends. There is no reliable water anywhere above the creek crossings low on the trail, so carry what you need from the forest crossings unless you are dropping into the basin below the East Peak, where a creek runs.

waypoints.name: Basin below the East Peak
waypoints.note: Drop roughly 300 ft over steep, slick vegetation into this basin; a creek provides the best water and camping on the route before the final push.
waypoints.directions: The end of the trail overlooks a basin to the east, directly under the East Peak. Getting into it means dropping roughly 300 ft down steep, densely vegetated ground that is treacherously slick when wet — this drop, and regaining it on the way out, is the hardest ground of the day to move on. A creek runs through the basin bottom.

waypoints.name: Summit gully
waypoints.note: Class 2 gully narrows with exposure dropping away on both sides near the top; stay centered in the gully rather than skirting the edges.
waypoints.directions: Cross the creek and head up toward the East Peak, picking up an easy class 2 gully. Snow lingers in it into summer, so carry an axe and be ready to self-arrest. Near the top the gully narrows and the ground falls away on both sides — stay centred in it rather than drifting out onto the edges.

waypoints.name: Goat Mountain, East Peak (true summit)
waypoints.note: Rocky, narrow summit spine dropping off steeply on all sides; USGS Mount Sefrit quad benchmark, higher than the West Peak across the basin.
waypoints.directions: Finish up the gully onto the summit spine. It is narrow and rocky, drops off steeply on every side, and the rock near the top is loose.

row.approach: From the Goat Mountain Trailhead (day-use parking just off FS-32/Hannegan Pass Rd, ~2.1-2.3 mi up from the Glacier Public Service Center), follow Goat Mountain Trail #673. It's a well-built but relentlessly steep trail that gains the ridge via dozens of switchbacks, crossing a small cascading creek/waterfall repeatedly in the first mile through old-growth fir and hemlock (look for ~100-year-old fire-scarred cedar snags). Around 1 mi (~3,200 ft) the grade eases and the trail traverses onto a narrow side-hill ridge. At roughly 2 mi the trail crosses into Mount Baker Wilderness; just past the boundary sign an unsigned spur ('Old Goat Trail') splits east toward an old lookout site - stay on the main tread. Big views of Baker, Shuksan, and Sefrit open through meadows by 2.7 mi, and the maintained trail tops out on the ridge crest at a 5,200-ft viewpoint knob around mile 4, with the official terminus near 5,600 ft (~4.1 mi, ~3,100 ft gain). Beyond this point the route leaves maintained tread and becomes an open ridge boot path: continue about 0.8 mi and 1,000 ft more to the ~6,600-ft West Peak false summit. Snow lingers here well into summer (reports note solid snow from ~4,300-4,500 ft), so carry an ice axe from around that elevation upward, and expect crampons or snowshoes to be useful in early/late season. Do not push straight over the false summit's top - it corniced and exposed; bypass it on the south or west slope. Past the false summit the ridge drops roughly 300 ft into a notch/col, then climbs the final stretch of mixed snow, rock, and short exposed steps to the true (East) summit at 6,892 ft. A narrow, moderately exposed knife-edge-ish section near the top is the crux of the scramble - keep the axe in hand and self-arrest-ready on the steep snow. There is no reliable water source beyond the creek crossings in the forest (roughly the first 2.5 miles of trail); carry what you need for the ridge and summit push.
row.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling anywhere on the route - reverse the ascent line exactly. Downclimb the mixed snow/rock crux back to the col, climb back over (or bypass around, staying off the cornices) the West Peak false summit, and regain the boot path down to the official trail terminus near 5,600 ft. From there, follow Goat Mountain Trail #673's switchbacks back down through the meadows, past the wilderness-boundary/Old Goat Trail junction, and through the old-growth section to the trailhead. Carry an ice axe and know self-arrest for both directions of travel on the snow sections: afternoon sun can soften the snowfields significantly (increasing slip and post-holing risk on the way down), while morning refreeze can leave the same slopes firm enough to want careful cramponing. Give cornices along the ridge crest a wide margin on the way down as well - they are easy to underestimate from above and have caused parties to detour off-route.
row.bail: Reversible at any point on the nontechnical terrain.

pitch_detail.notes: Established trail through old-growth forest with switchbacks. ~5 miles roundtrip to maintained trail terminus (5,400 feet). Forest section may be muddy in late spring.
Off-trail scrambling through heather, talus, and alpine meadow. Route-finding required. Climbing directly toward snowfield below West Peak. Loose talus requires careful footing.
Steep permanent snowfield traverse (~400-500 vertical feet) requiring ice axe and crampons/microspikes. This is the crux pitch; fall here is potentially fatal. Angle ~40-45 degrees.
Summit scramble on exposed Class 2-3 terrain with some exposure. Final 100-150 vertical feet to the East Peak summit. No technical rock climbing but scrambling is exposed with 500+ foot drops nearby.

itinerary.cal: A permanent snowfield often lingers near the summit gully into summer, so many parties carry an ice axe even late in the season.

days.note: This is a single long day, not a backpack — parties leave the Hannegan Pass Road trailhead (~2,500 ft) before dawn, climb the maintained Goat Mountain Trail #673 through forest into heather/huckleberry meadows, then follow unmaintained tread and open slopes to a saddle below the false summit before dropping and re-climbing to the East Peak via an exposed Class 2 gully. Most parties are back at the car by early evening.

climate.typical: Marine west coast climate: Pacific frontal systems bring heavy precipitation, especially November-March, with orographic lift off the Cascades increasing winter snowfall. Summers (July-September) are the driest and clearest, often with little or no cloud cover.

bySeason.summer: July-September is the prime window; the south-facing trail is typically snow-free earlier than most other Mt. Baker Highway hikes, though small snow patches can linger on the shaded ridge crest into early July.
bySeason.winter: FS-32 is closed to vehicles; the lower road corridor is a popular beginner ski-touring/snowshoe area.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Goat Mountain Trailhead (day-use parking just off FS-32/Hannegan Pass Rd, ~2.1-2.3 mi up from the Glacier Public Service Center), follow Goat Mountain Trail #673.

approach_variants.name: Goat Mountain Trail #673 to the end of maintained tread, then over the West Peak false summit
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goat Mountain Trailhead, day-use parking just off FS-32 (Hannegan Pass Road) about 2.1-2.5 miles up from the Glacier Public Service Center, follow Goat Mountain Trail #673. It is well built and relentlessly steep, gaining the ridge by dozens of switchbacks and crossing a small cascading creek repeatedly in the first mile through old-growth fir and hemlock.

Around a mile in, near 3,200 ft, the grade eases and the trail traverses a narrow side-hill ridge. At roughly two miles it crosses into the Mount Baker Wilderness; just past the boundary sign an unsigned spur — the Old Goat Trail — splits east toward an old lookout site. Stay on the main tread.

Meadows and big views open by 2.7 miles; the maintained trail tops out on the crest at a 5,200 ft viewpoint knob around mile 4, with the official terminus near 5,600 ft.

Beyond that it is an open ridge boot path, about 0.8 mile and 1,000 ft more to the West Peak false summit near 6,600 ft, and then on to the true East summit.

There is no reliable water beyond the creek crossings in the forest, roughly the first 2.5 miles of trail.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow lingers on this ridge and reports have found solid snow from 4,300-4,500 ft well into summer
hazards: Cornices on the West Peak false summit, invisible from above
Solid lingering snow from 4,300-4,500 ft upward well into summer
A knife-edge-ish exposed section near the true summit
No reliable water beyond the forest creek crossings (about the first 2.5 miles)
An unsigned spur trail near the wilderness boundary that leads to an old lookout site instead
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS WHERE THE MAINTAINED TRAIL STOPS, NEAR 5,600 FT, AND THAT END IS ABRUPT. Below it, built tread and switchbacks. Above it, an open ridge boot path with nothing constructed. If you are still on graded trail you have not started the route.

THE FALSE SUMMIT IS CORNICED — DO NOT GO OVER ITS TOP. This is the one hard rule on the ridge and it is a safety instruction rather than a route preference: the West Peak at about 6,600 ft is corniced and exposed, and the correct line bypasses it on the SOUTH or WEST slope. Cornices are invisible from above and this is precisely the terrain where cloud sits.

THE 300 FT DROP IS HOW YOU KNOW YOU HAVE PASSED THE FALSE SUMMIT, AND IT IS THE STRONGEST TEST ON THE ROUTE. Past the West Peak the ridge DROPS ROUGHLY 300 FT into a notch before climbing again. So: if you have not descended 300 ft, the high ground in front of you is not the true summit — it is the false one you were supposed to walk around. An altimeter settles this in zero visibility and eyesight does not.

AFTER THE NOTCH it is a final stretch of mixed snow, rock and short exposed steps to the true East summit at 6,892 ft. The crux is a narrow, moderately exposed knife-edge-ish section near the top — keep the axe in hand and self-arrest-ready on the steep snow.

CARRY THE AXE FROM 4,300-4,500 FT, not from where the snow looks serious. That is where reports put the solid snow, and it is well below the point where a party without an axe realises it wanted one.

climbing_route.label: Open ridge boot path to the West Peak false summit
climbing_route.notes: Beyond the official trail terminus near 5,600 ft the route leaves maintained tread for an open ridge boot path: about 0.8 mi and 1,000 ft more to the ~6,600-ft West Peak false summit. Snow lingers well into summer (reports note solid snow from ~4,300-4,500 ft), so carry an ice axe from around that elevation upward, and expect crampons or snowshoes to be useful in early/late season.

climbing_route.label: False summit bypass
climbing_route.notes: Do not push straight over the false summit's top — it is corniced and exposed; bypass it on the south or west slope.

climbing_route.label: Notch/col and the final ridge to the East summit
climbing_route.notes: Past the false summit the ridge drops roughly 300 ft into a notch/col, then climbs the final stretch of mixed snow, rock, and short exposed steps to the true (East) summit at 6,892 ft.

climbing_route.label: Knife-edge crux near the top
climbing_route.notes: A narrow, moderately exposed knife-edge-ish section near the top is the crux of the scramble — keep the axe in hand and self-arrest-ready on the steep snow. No reliable water beyond the creek crossings in the forest, roughly the first 2.5 miles of trail.

bivy.name: Open benches on the broad ridge
bivy.notes: The best camping on the mountain if you are willing to haul water, and the natural base for the south ridge scramble. A series of level shelves on a broad, open ridge above treeline, past a viewpoint knob near 5,200 ft, with Baker, Shuksan and Sefrit filling the skyline and the Border Peaks and the Pickets beyond. From here the maintained trail continues to its end on the shoulder and the scramble to the summits goes on from there, so a camp at the benches leaves a short and pleasant summit morning. The slope faces south and melts early, so this is usually accessible from late June, sometimes earlier; the trade is that it bakes and stays dry all summer. It is fully exposed to wind and to weather rolling in from the west with nothing to duck behind. Excellent huckleberries in early autumn, and bears know it.
bivy.water: NONE. Everything must be carried up from the last crossing in the forest. Snow patches linger into July in shaded pockets and can be melted early in the season, but by August the whole crest is dry
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass at the trailhead. No campfires. Camp on bare ground, gravel or an existing flat rather than in the heather, and store food securely against bears
bivy.capacity: Two or three small tents spread across the benches, kept apart so the heather is not trampled into one bare patch

bivy.name: Last stream crossing, top of the forest
bivy.notes: Listed for the water rather than for the camping, and the water is the point. The trail climbs steeply from the trailhead through about a dozen switchbacks in the first mile and stays in deep forest for two and a half, crossing several small creeks on the way; the highest of them sits right where the trees thin into heather and huckleberry. Above this line the mountain gives you nothing. Parties heading to the benches or the crest should stop here, top up, and accept carrying the weight for the last stretch. Late in a dry summer even these crossings run thin, so do not assume the lower ones are still flowing on the way down. Elevation is not stated because the exact crossing shifts with the season and the snowpack; navigate to it by the transition out of the timber, not by an altimeter reading.
bivy.water: THIS IS THE LAST RELIABLE WATER ON THE MOUNTAIN, at roughly mile 2.7 where the final creeks cross the tread. Treat it. Everything on the ridge above is dry, so fill every container here whether or not you intend to camp
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, whose boundary the trail crosses around mile 2. No overnight permit is required and none is issued. Twelve-person party limit. Campfires are not permitted on this trail, so carry a stove. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required at the trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is not valid here. Black bears work this slope in huckleberry season and food must be secured overnight
bivy.capacity: One or two tents on rough ground beside the trail where the timber gives out; there is no established site and the slope is steep, so flat spots are few

bivy.name: Ridge crest at the end of the maintained trail
bivy.notes: The highest ground with anything like a flat pitch, where the maintained trail ends on Goat Mountain's shoulder and the route becomes a steep boot path up grass and heather to the false summit and the west peak. The crest carries on upward from here toward 5,600 ft and above, and the east peak, which is the higher of the two, is a further meadow scramble along the ridge with no trail. Camping here shortens summit day to almost nothing, which is the only argument for it: it is stony, cramped and completely exposed, and it is the driest spot on a dry mountain. Snow can lie across the upper slope into July and the grass traverse above is genuinely slippery when wet, so this is a fair-weather choice. Sunrise and sunset from the crest are the reason people put up with all of it.
bivy.water: NONE, and the nearest is the forest crossings far below. In early season there are snow patches on the north side of the crest to melt; from midsummer there is nothing at all
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit, twelve-person limit, recreation pass at the trailhead, no campfires. This is national forest rather than national park — the park boundary lies well east beyond Hannegan Pass — so no park backcountry permit applies
bivy.capacity: One or two tents on the shoulder where the tread runs out; small, stony and windy

bivy.name: Basin below the east peak
bivy.notes: The one camp on Goat Mountain that solves the water problem, in the basin lying east and below the higher east peak, seen from the overlook near the top of the maintained trail. It has ample flat terrain and running water, which nothing on the ridge does. The cost is that reaching it means leaving the trail entirely and dropping off the crest on trackless ground, which is more commitment than most parties want for a scramble that can be done in a day from the benches — so it is chosen mainly by people camping two nights, going for the east summit as well as the west, or arriving too late in the season for the crest to hold snow. Approach it from the end of the maintained trail rather than trying to contour in low. No elevation is given because the usable ground spreads across the basin floor rather than sitting at one identifiable spot.
bivy.water: Present, which makes this basin unique here — snowmelt streams and pools that last well into the season, unlike anything on the crest. Treat it, and check that it is still running before relying on it in a dry late summer
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass at the trailhead, no campfires. Camp on durable ground away from the water and secure food overnight
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents with room to spread out; the most generous ground on the mountain
